45: // has two server blocks to start with. But expressed in this Caddyfile are
46: // actually 4 listener addresses: 127.0.0.1:443, 1.2.3.4:443, 127.0.0.1:9999,
47: // and 127.0.0.1:9999. This is because the bind directive is applied to each
48: // key of its server block (specifying the host part), and each key may have
49: // a different port. And we definitely need to be sure that a site which is
50: // bound to be served on a specific interface is not served on others just
51: // because that is more convenient: it would be a potential security risk
52: // if the difference between interfaces means private vs. public.
53: //
54: // So what this function does for the example above is iterate each server
55: // block, and for each server block, iterate its keys. For the first, it
56: // finds one key (example.com) and determines its listener address
57: // (127.0.0.1:443 - because of 'bind' and automatic HTTPS). It then adds
58: // the listener address to the map value returned by this function, with
59: // the first server block as one of its associations.
60: //
61: // It then iterates each key on the second server block and associates them
62: // with one or more listener addresses. Indeed, each key in this block has
63: // two listener addresses because of the 'bind' directive. Once we know
64: // which addresses serve which keys, we can create a new server block for
65: // each address containing the contents of the server block and only those
66: // specific keys of the server block which use that address.
67: //
68: // It is possible and even likely that some keys in the returned map have
69: // the exact same list of server blocks (i.e. they are identical). This
70: // happens when multiple hosts are declared with a 'bind' directive and
71: // the resulting listener addresses are not shared by any other server
72: // block (or the other server blocks are exactly identical in their token
73: // contents). This happens with our example above because 1.2.3.4:443
74: // and 1.2.3.4:9999 are used exclusively with the second server block. This
75: // repetition may be undesirable, so call consolidateAddrMappings() to map
76: // multiple addresses to the same lists of server blocks (a many:many mapping).
77: // (Doing this is essentially a map-reduce technique.)
78: func (st *ServerType) mapAddressToServerBlocks(originalServerBlocks []serverBlock,
79: 	options map[string]interface{}) (map[string][]serverBlock, error) {
80: 	sbmap := make(map[string][]serverBlock)
81: 
82: 	for i, sblock := range originalServerBlocks {
83: 		// within a server block, we need to map all the listener addresses
84: 		// implied by the server block to the keys of the server block which
85: 		// will be served by them; this has the effect of treating each
86: 		// key of a server block as its own, but without having to repeat its
87: 		// contents in cases where multiple keys really can be served together
88: 		addrToKeys := make(map[string][]string)
89: 		for j, key := range sblock.block.Keys {
90: 			// a key can have multiple listener addresses if there are multiple
91: 			// arguments to the 'bind' directive (although they will all have
92: 			// the same port, since the port is defined by the key or is implicit
93: 			// through automatic HTTPS)
94: 			addrs, err := st.listenerAddrsForServerBlockKey(sblock, key, options)
95: 			if err != nil {
96: 				return nil, fmt.Errorf("server block %d, key %d (%s): determining listener address: %v", i, j, key, err)
97: 			}
98: 
99: 			// associate this key with each listener address it is served on
100: 			for _, addr := range addrs {
101: 				addrToKeys[addr] = append(addrToKeys[addr], key)
102: 			}
103: 		}
104: 
105: 		// now that we know which addresses serve which keys of this
106: 		// server block, we iterate that mapping and create a list of
107: 		// new server blocks for each address where the keys of the
108: 		// server block are only the ones which use the address; but
109: 		// the contents (tokens) are of course the same
110: 		for addr, keys := range addrToKeys {
111: 			// parse keys so that we only have to do it once
112: 			parsedKeys := make([]Address, 0, len(keys))
113: 			for _, key := range keys {
114: 				addr, err := ParseAddress(key)
115: 				if err != nil {
116: 					return nil, fmt.Errorf("parsing key '%s': %v", key, err)
117: 				}
118: 				parsedKeys = append(parsedKeys, addr.Normalize())
119: 			}
120: 			sbmap[addr] = append(sbmap[addr], serverBlock{
121: 				block: caddyfile.ServerBlock{
122: 					Keys:     keys,
123: 					Segments: sblock.block.Segments,
124: 				},
125: 				pile: sblock.pile,
126: 				keys: parsedKeys,
127: 			})
128: 		}
129: 	}
130: 
131: 	return sbmap, nil
132: }
133: 
134: // consolidateAddrMappings eliminates repetition of identical server blocks in a mapping of
135: // single listener addresses to lists of server blocks. Since multiple addresses may serve
136: // identical sites (server block contents), this function turns a 1:many mapping into a
137: // many:many mapping. Server block contents (tokens) must be exactly identical so that
138: // reflect.DeepEqual returns true in order for the addresses to be combined. Identical
139: // entries are deleted from the addrToServerBlocks map. Essentially, each pairing (each
140: // association from multiple addresses to multiple server blocks; i.e. each element of
141: // the returned slice) becomes a server definition in the output JSON.
142: func (st *ServerType) consolidateAddrMappings(addrToServerBlocks map[string][]serverBlock) []sbAddrAssociation {
143: 	sbaddrs := make([]sbAddrAssociation, 0, len(addrToServerBlocks))
144: 	for addr, sblocks := range addrToServerBlocks {
145: 		// we start with knowing that at least this address
146: 		// maps to these server blocks
147: 		a := sbAddrAssociation{
148: 			addresses:    []string{addr},
149: 			serverBlocks: sblocks,
150: 		}
151: 
152: 		// now find other addresses that map to identical
153: 		// server blocks and add them to our list of
154: 		// addresses, while removing them from the map
155: 		for otherAddr, otherSblocks := range addrToServerBlocks {
156: 			if addr == otherAddr {
157: 				continue
158: 			}
159: 			if reflect.DeepEqual(sblocks, otherSblocks) {
160: 				a.addresses = append(a.addresses, otherAddr)
161: 				delete(addrToServerBlocks, otherAddr)
162: 			}
163: 		}
164: 
165: 		sbaddrs = append(sbaddrs, a)
166: 	}
167: 
168: 	// sort them by their first address (we know there will always be at least one)
169: 	// to avoid problems with non-deterministic ordering (makes tests flaky)
170: 	sort.Slice(sbaddrs, func(i, j int) bool {
171: 		return sbaddrs[i].addresses[0] < sbaddrs[j].addresses[0]
172: 	})
173: 
174: 	return sbaddrs
175: }
176:

180: 	addrInput := key
181: 	if len(addrInput) > maxAddrLen {

part.text:
Implemented multi-address `default_bind` support.

- `default_bind` now parses all arguments on its line as `[]string`.
- Sites without an explicit `bind` apply every configured default bind address.
- Listener-address consolidation now sorts combined addresses for deterministic adapted JSON output.

Validated in the supplied container:

- `go test ./caddyconfig/httpcaddyfile`
- `go test ./caddytest/integration -run TestCaddyfileAdaptToJSON`
- `git diff --check`
